easy.prompt: A single perceptron computes its output by taking inputs x, weights w, and bias b and then doing what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Weighted sum of inputs plus bias, then a nonlinear activation: y = σ(w·x + b).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Median of the inputs, ignoring all learned weights.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Product of all inputs with no bias term added.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Count of nonzero inputs, with no activation function.

easy.hint: Start with w·x + b, then ask what wraps that sum to add nonlinearity.
easy.explanation: A perceptron forms an affine combination of inputs and passes it through an activation function.
easy.deepDive: The weighted sum lets the neuron weight features differently, and the bias shifts the decision threshold. The activation adds nonlinearity so networks can learn curves, not just lines. Without learned weights the unit could not adapt to data at all.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Neurons learn weights; they never sort inputs or take medians.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Perceptrons sum weighted inputs; pure products are not the affine form.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Counting nonzero inputs ignores continuous values and learned parameters.

easy.prompt: Perceptron with w=2, b=0, ReLU activation, input x=1. What is the output?

choices.label: C
choices.body: 1+0 = 1 regardless of the weight value.

choices.label: D
choices.body: 2(1) = 2 with no bias and no activation applied.

easy.hint: Compute z = wx+b first, then apply max(0,z).
easy.explanation: First compute z = 2·1+0 = 2, then ReLU(z) = max(0,2) = 2.
easy.deepDive: Compute the affine part first: 2 times 1 plus 0 equals 2. ReLU keeps every nonnegative value unchanged, so the output is 2. This two-step pattern of affine map then activation repeats in every MLP layer.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ReLU zeroes negatives, not positives; ReLU(2) is 2.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The weight multiplies the input; you cannot drop it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The MLP unit always applies its activation after the affine step.

easy.prompt: Perceptron with w=1, b=−2, ReLU activation, input x=1. What is the output?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 0 because the bias shifts the sum below zero.

choices.label: B
choices.body: −1 because ReLU flips the sign of negatives.

choices.label: C
choices.body: −1 passed through unchanged since ReLU is linear.

choices.label: D
choices.body: 1 because bias is always ignored at test time.

easy.hint: Compute z = 1·1 − 2, then apply max(0,z).
easy.deepDive: The affine value is 1·1+(−2) = −1. ReLU outputs max(0,−1) = 0, which models a unit that stays silent until its input is strong enough. The bias acts as a threshold the weighted input must overcome.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ReLU never flips signs; it zeroes negatives.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ReLU is piecewise nonlinear, not the identity on negatives.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bias is part of every forward pass, train and test.

easy.prompt: Which architecture is a multilayer perceptron (MLP)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A stack of hidden layers that repeatedly applies affine maps plus nonlinearities.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A single neuron with no hidden layers at all.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A lookup table that memorizes pixel means.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A clustering step followed by label sorting.

easy.hint: Think layers of (linear + σ) repeated: what sits between input and output?
easy.explanation: An MLP stacks affine transforms with a nonlinearity after each hidden layer.
easy.deepDive: Each hidden layer transforms the previous representation, so deeper layers compose simpler features into abstract ones. One layer alone is limited in the functions it can compactly express. Depth with nonlinearity is what gives MLPs their expressive power.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is a single perceptron, not a multilayer network.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: MLPs learn parametric maps; they are not memorized tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: MLPs do supervised function approximation, not clustering plus sorting.

easy.prompt: Two hidden layers with NO activation functions collapse to the power of which simpler model?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Stacking linear layers without any activation between them.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Adding ReLU after each hidden affine transform.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Adding one hidden layer with a nonlinear activation.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Widening a hidden layer while keeping its activation.

easy.hint: Multiply two matrices in your head: how many matrices is the result?
easy.explanation: Composing affine maps yields one affine map, so depth without nonlinearity adds no power.
easy.deepDive: A product of matrices is still one matrix, so W2(W1x) equals some single Wx regardless of depth. Nonlinearities break this collapse by bending the space between layers. That is why every hidden layer needs its σ.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ReLU between layers prevents collapse; that adds real depth.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One nonlinear hidden layer is already a universal approximator setup.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Widening with activations keeps genuine nonlinear capacity.

easy.prompt: A 10-layer MLP with all activations removed is exactly equivalent to what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A linear model no more powerful than one layer.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A universal approximator for any continuous function.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A convex optimization problem with one global minimum.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A model that no longer needs labeled targets.

easy.hint: Ask what W3·W2·W1 simplifies to as one object.
easy.explanation: Without activations the whole stack is a single affine map.
easy.deepDive: Linear maps compose into linear maps, so ten linear layers equal one matrix multiply. The network can only draw straight decision boundaries. Only inserting nonlinear activations lets depth build hierarchical features.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Universality requires nonlinear hidden units; linear stacks cannot bend.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Deep linear or nonlinear nets are generally non-convex in weights.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Supervision still needs labels; linearity changes capacity, not data needs.

easy.prompt: During training, what do the forward pass and the loss function each do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Forward pass predicts; loss compares prediction to target.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Forward pass updates weights directly from labels.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Forward pass shuffles labels to decorrelate batches.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Forward pass skips the output layer entirely.

easy.hint: Separate inference (inputs→prediction) from scoring (prediction vs target).
easy.explanation: Forward propagation turns inputs into predictions, and the loss scores them.
easy.deepDive: Activations flow from input toward the output layer, producing ŷ for each example. The loss ℓ(ŷ,y) then scores how far predictions are from targets. Gradients of that score later drive the backward pass.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Weights change only after the backward pass and optimizer step.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Labels are fixed targets; forward pass never permutes them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The output layer produces the predictions being scored.

easy.prompt: For regression with target y=2 and prediction ŷ=5, which loss gives (5−2)²=9 before averaging?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Mean squared error: average of (prediction − target)².

choices.label: B
choices.body: Accuracy counted with no differentiable formula.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The raw weight matrix with no targets involved.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The learning rate divided by batch size.

easy.hint: Write (ŷ−y)² per example, then average: which choice matches?
easy.explanation: Regression typically minimizes average squared residual.
easy.deepDive: Squaring penalizes large errors more than small ones and keeps the objective smooth for gradients. Averaging over the batch stabilizes the estimate. Classification more often uses cross-entropy, but squared error is the canonical regression loss.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Accuracy is a metric, not a differentiable training loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Loss must compare predictions against targets, not list weights.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Learning rate and batch size configure optimization, not the loss value.

easy.prompt: For image classification with softmax outputs, the standard training loss is what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cross-entropy between predicted probabilities and true labels.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The number of hidden layers in the network.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The sum of all inputs ignoring the labels.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The variance of the raw pixels only.

easy.hint: Ask what compares a probability vector against the true class.
easy.explanation: Classification trains on negative log-likelihood of the correct class.
easy.deepDive: Cross-entropy rewards probability mass on the correct class and heavily penalizes confident wrong answers. It pairs naturally with a softmax output. Squared error is possible but optimizes probability calibration less directly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Depth is architecture, not the objective being minimized.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Loss must involve labels; inputs alone define no error.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Pixel variance is data statistics, not prediction error.

easy.prompt: What gradient does a mini-batch SGD update use?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Average gradient over a random subset of B examples: one noisy but cheap step.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exact full-dataset gradient recomputed over all N examples every step.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Gradient of a single weight coordinate with all others frozen.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Closed-form optimum solved without any gradients.

easy.hint: Write (1/B)·Σ∇ℓᵢ over which index set: all N or a subset B?
easy.explanation: Mini-batch SGD estimates the true gradient from a small random batch.
easy.deepDive: Averaging B examples cuts gradient noise versus single-sample SGD while staying far cheaper than full-batch sums. The noise itself can help escape sharp minima. Batch size B trades hardware throughput against update freshness.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is full-batch gradient descent, not mini-batch SGD.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SGD updates all parameters jointly, not one coordinate at a time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Deep nets use iterative gradient steps, not closed-form solves.

easy.prompt: What is one training iteration (step) versus one epoch?

choices.label: A
choices.body: One parameter update from one mini-batch: forward, backward, optimizer step.

choices.label: B
choices.body: One full pass over the entire training set.

choices.label: C
choices.body: One evaluation sweep over the test set.

choices.label: D
choices.body: One reshuffling of files on disk.

easy.hint: Ask what triggers one optimizer step: one batch or the whole dataset?
easy.explanation: An iteration is a single mini-batch update; an epoch is a full data pass.
easy.deepDive: Each iteration consumes one batch and applies one optimizer step. An epoch groups enough iterations to cover the dataset once. Counting iterations versus epochs matters when comparing schedules and wall-clock budgets.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A full pass is an epoch, which contains many iterations.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Evaluation performs no parameter updates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Shuffling is bookkeeping; the update defines the iteration.

easy.prompt: Compared with large batches, small mini-batches give what trade-off?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Noisier per-step estimates with more frequent updates per epoch.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exact gradients with fewer updates per epoch.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deterministic closed-form solutions each step.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Frozen weights that never change size.

easy.hint: Fix the dataset size, shrink B: does the step count per epoch rise or fall?
easy.explanation: Smaller batches mean noisier but more frequent updates.
easy.deepDive: Small batches estimate the gradient from fewer samples, so each step is noisier. But they yield more steps per epoch and often better generalization. Large batches give cleaner estimates at the cost of fewer updates and more memory.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Exact gradients need the full dataset, not small batches.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Mini-batch training stays stochastic and iterative.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Weights update every step regardless of batch size.

easy.prompt: What is the vanilla SGD parameter update given gradient g = ∇L?

choices.label: A
choices.body: w ← w − η∇L: step against the gradient scaled by η.

choices.label: B
choices.body: w ← w + η∇L: step along the gradient uphill.

choices.label: C
choices.body: w ← random new values ignoring the gradient.

choices.label: D
choices.body: w ← w/η with no gradient involved.

easy.hint: The gradient points uphill: which sign moves downhill?
easy.explanation: SGD steps parameters opposite the gradient direction.
easy.deepDive: The gradient points toward steepest ascent, so descent steps opposite to it. The learning rate η sets the stride length along that direction. Repeating small downhill steps traces a path toward a local minimum.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Adding the gradient ascends the loss instead of minimizing it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Random resets discard all gradient information.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Dividing by η without the gradient ignores the loss landscape.

easy.prompt: If the learning rate is far too large, what training symptom appears?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Oscillating or diverging loss from overshooting minima.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Instant one-step convergence to zero loss.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Gradients that become exactly zero everywhere.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Doubled dataset size after each epoch.

easy.hint: Picture stepping over a narrow valley: do you land inside it or beyond it?
easy.explanation: Too-large learning rates overshoot and destabilize training.
easy.deepDive: Steps larger than the local curvature allows jump across valleys instead of settling in. The loss then bounces or explodes as weights swing wildly. Reducing η or adding scheduling restores stable descent.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Huge steps rarely land exactly on a minimum.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Zero gradients mean saturation or convergence, not large steps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Learning rate never changes the number of examples.

easy.prompt: If the learning rate is far too small, what training symptom appears?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Painfully slow progress with loss creeping down tiny amounts.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Immediate divergence to NaN loss.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Automatic growth of the network width.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Gradients that reverse direction every batch.

easy.hint: Take a tiny stride toward a far goal: how many strides do you need?
easy.explanation: Too-small learning rates converge but waste compute on tiny moves.
easy.deepDive: Tiny steps move safely downhill but cover little distance per update. Training then needs far more epochs to reach good loss. The fix is raising η or adding momentum and schedules rather than accepting the crawl.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: NaNs come from too-large steps or instability, not tiny ones.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Learning rate cannot add neurons to the architecture.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Direction comes from gradients; small η only shrinks stride length.

easy.prompt: What does the learning rate control, and does Adam remove the need to tune it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Step size per update; tuned via loss curves and schedules.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Number of layers in the network.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Number of classes in the dataset.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Size of each input image in pixels.

easy.hint: Which knob multiplies the gradient in w − ηg?
easy.explanation: Learning rate scales each gradient step and critically affects training.
easy.deepDive: The learning rate multiplies every gradient step, so it controls speed and stability directly. Too high diverges while too low crawls. Practitioners grid-search it first because no optimizer fully removes its influence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Depth is set by architecture, not by the step-size scalar.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Class count is fixed by the task labels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Image size is data geometry, not an optimization stride.

easy.prompt: What is the purpose of decaying the learning rate during training?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Bigger steps early for progress, smaller steps late for fine convergence.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Constant huge steps from start to finish.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Zero learning rate after the first epoch.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Random shuffling of labels each epoch.

easy.hint: Think coarse search first, fine adjustment last: how should η evolve?
easy.explanation: Learning-rate schedules decay step size as training progresses.
easy.deepDive: Large early steps traverse broad loss terrain quickly. Decaying later prevents bouncing around sharp minima. Schedules like step, cosine, or warmup-plus-decay automate this SCOUR pattern across epochs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Constant huge steps overshoot once near a minimum.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Zero LR freezes learning entirely after epoch one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Label shuffling corrupts supervision; it is not a schedule.

easy.prompt: What is learning-rate warmup and why is it used?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Warmup: start η small and ramp up before decaying.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Instant maximum η on the very first batch.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Freezing all weights for the first epochs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Deleting the first 10% of training data.

easy.hint: If step 1 is the noisiest, should η start big or small?
easy.explanation: Warmup avoids early instability from noisy gradients and biased moments.
easy.deepDive: Early gradients are noisy and adaptive moment estimates start at zero, so full-size steps can destabilize. Ramping η lets statistics stabilize before aggressive descent. Transformers and large-batch training rely on warmup especially heavily.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Maximum-first steps amplify early instability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Freezing wastes early epochs instead of gently ramping steps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Dropping data does not fix early optimization instability.

easy.prompt: Compared with a fully connected layer on images, a convolution uses what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Local receptive fields with shared filters slid across positions.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A unique weight for every input-output pair globally.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only 1×1 kernels that never mix neighbors.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Fixed random filters never updated by training.

easy.hint: Contrast per-pixel-pair weights against one small filter reused everywhere.
easy.explanation: Convolution uses local shared weights, unlike dense global weights.
easy.deepDive: Local connectivity exploits the fact that nearby pixels correlate most strongly. Sharing one filter across positions detects the same feature anywhere and slashes parameters. The result is translation-friendly feature maps learned from data.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes a dense layer on flattened pixels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Typical kernels are 3×3 or 5×5 and mix neighborhoods.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Conv filters are learned parameters updated by backprop.

easy.prompt: How is an RGB image represented going into the first conv layer?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Height × Width × 3 channels, plus a batch dim for mini-batches.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A single scalar brightness value.

choices.label: C
choices.body: One 3×3 matrix shared across all datasets.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sequence-length × vocabulary-size token grid.

easy.hint: Count color planes: how many spatial grids does one color image hold?
easy.explanation: RGB images are three aligned spatial maps of color intensity.
easy.deepDive: Each color channel forms a spatial map aligned with the others pixel-for-pixel. Convolutions slide over height and width while summing across all three channels. Mini-batches stack several such tensors along a leading batch axis.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Images are spatial grids, not single numbers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 3×3 may be kernel size; channels are separate feature maps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That layout describes NLP token inputs, not raw images.

easy.prompt: Why is zero-padding used before a convolution?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Controls output size by adding border pixels so edges stay covered.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Converts RGB to grayscale automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Guarantees training loss reaches exactly zero.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Replaces backprop with a closed-form solve.

easy.hint: What happens to border pixels when a 3×3 kernel overhangs the edge?
easy.explanation: Zero-padding preserves spatial dimensions and edge information.
easy.deepDive: Without padding, each conv shrinks the map and discards edge context. Same-padding adds rings of zeros to preserve H×W through the layer. Valid-padding skips the border and lets the map shrink instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Channel conversion is separate preprocessing, not padding.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Padding changes geometry, not loss optimality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Training still needs gradient-based updates.

easy.prompt: What does 2×2 max pooling with stride 2 do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Halves height and width, keeping the strongest response per 2×2 region.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Doubles the number of channels.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Takes a weighted sum over the whole image.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Applies a learnable 3×3 kernel everywhere.

easy.hint: Slide a 2×2 window with step 2: how many outputs per 4 pixels?
easy.explanation: 2×2 stride-2 max pool downsamples spatially via local maxima.
easy.deepDive: Max pooling outputs the maximum activation inside each non-overlapping window. Stride 2 steps window-to-window without overlap, halving each spatial dim. Channel count is untouched because pooling acts per channel independently.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Pooling never changes channel count by itself.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is global average pooling, not local max pooling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Pooling has no learnable weights; that describes convolution.

easy.prompt: Does max/average pooling learn weights?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No learnable weights; fixed downsampling with no gradients to learn.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Learnable 3×3 kernels updated by backprop.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Per-channel scale and shift learned like batchnorm.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Attention weights computed from queries and keys.

easy.hint: Ask which layer has filter weights for the optimizer to change.
easy.explanation: Pooling is parameter-free, unlike convolution.
easy.deepDive: Pooling applies a fixed max or average rule inside each window. There are no filter parameters for the optimizer to update. Learning spatial features is the convolution's job; pooling only compresses the map.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes conv layers, not pooling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Scale/shift parameters belong to normalization layers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: QKV attention weights are a transformer mechanism.

easy.prompt: How does average pooling differ from max pooling?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Average of each window: smoother, keeps background context.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Maximum of each window: keeps strongest activation.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Learned weighted sum with per-window filters.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Median over the entire dataset at once.

easy.hint: Mean versus max: which keeps the whole window's information?
easy.explanation: Average pooling smooths each region instead of selecting peaks.
easy.deepDive: Averaging blends all pixels in the window, preserving diffuse texture and background. Max pooling instead keeps only the sharpest feature response. Modern nets often replace either with strided convolutions that learn the downsampling.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the definition of max pooling, not average.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Pooling windows have no learned filters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Pooling is per-image spatial, never dataset-wide.

easy.prompt: What is data augmentation for image training?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Plausible label-preserving variants (crops, flips) shown during training.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exact copies of test images leaked into training.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Random label shuffling to decorrelate batches.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Zeroing all parameters before each epoch.

easy.hint: Which option creates new training views without touching the test set?
easy.explanation: Augmentation diversifies training inputs while keeping labels valid.
easy.deepDive: A flipped cat is still a cat, so the augmented copy teaches invariance without new labels. Random crops, color jitter, and cutout multiply effective dataset size. Test data must stay unseen for the accuracy number to mean anything.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Leaking test data invalidates evaluation entirely.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Shuffling labels destroys supervision instead of diversifying inputs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Zeroing weights would erase all learned progress.

easy.prompt: What does a flatten (reshape) layer before a classifier head do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Flattens H×W×C feature maps into a 1D vector for dense layers.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Applies a 3×3 convolution with stride 2.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Max-pools across the whole dataset.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Adds sinusoidal position codes to pixels.

easy.hint: What shape change connects a 3D feature map to a 1D dense input?
easy.explanation: Flatten reshapes conv features into a vector for the classifier head.
easy.deepDive: Conv blocks output spatial tensors, but dense classifiers expect flat vectors. Flatten concatenates every spatial and channel entry in order. Global average pooling is the modern alternative that skips dense layers and cuts parameters.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is a strided conv, not a reshape.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Pooling is spatial downsampling, not batch-level flattening.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sinusoids are transformer positional encodings.

easy.prompt: What is transfer learning in vision CNNs?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Pretrained ImageNet weights reused, then fine-tuned on the target task.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Random init trained on three images only.

choices.label: C
choices.body: All conv layers deleted, pooling only.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Loss function frozen so it never changes.

easy.hint: Where do good edge detectors come from fastest: random or pretrained?
easy.explanation: Transfer learning reuses learned visual features for new tasks.
easy.deepDive: Early conv filters learn generic edges and textures that transfer across vision tasks. Starting from them beats random init especially on small datasets. Fine-tuning then adapts higher layers to the new classes with a small learning rate.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Three images cannot train a deep net; pretraining supplies the prior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Conv layers carry the transferable features; do not delete them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Weights adapt, not the loss definition.

easy.prompt: At each time step t, what does a vanilla RNN combine?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Current input x_t plus previous hidden state h_{t−1} to make h_t.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only x_t with no memory of earlier steps.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Future inputs x_{t+1}… before seeing x_t.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Independent predictions with no shared weights.

easy.hint: Which two vectors enter the recurrence at step t: now and what past?
easy.explanation: Vanilla RNNs carry summarized history forward via the hidden state.
easy.deepDive: The recurrence h_t = f(W_h h_{t−1} + W_x x_t + b) folds history into a fixed-size state. Sharing W_h and W_x across steps keeps parameters compact over long sequences. Without h_{t−1} the model would treat each step independently.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ignoring h_{t−1} reduces the model to per-step feedforward.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Causal RNNs never peek at future inputs at step t.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: RNNs share weights across all time steps.

easy.prompt: What information does the RNN hidden state h_t represent?

choices.label: A
choices.body: h_t summarizes x_1…x_t for predicting outputs at or after t.

choices.label: B
choices.body: h_t stores the entire future sequence in advance.

choices.label: C
choices.body: h_t is random noise unrelated to inputs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: h_t counts only dataset size, not content.

easy.hint: After processing t tokens, which prefix has the state seen?
easy.explanation: Hidden state is a compressed memory of the sequence prefix.
easy.deepDive: Each update blends new evidence with the running summary of everything before. Later predictions therefore condition on full prefix context through h_t. Fixed state size means old detail compresses and eventually fades, motivating gates and attention.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Causal states see the past, never the future.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: States are deterministic functions of inputs and prior state.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: State content encodes sequence content, not dataset size.

easy.prompt: What does 'unrolling' an RNN over time mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Unrolled length-T chain sharing one set of recurrent weights.

choices.label: B
choices.body: T unrelated networks with separate weights.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A single feedforward layer with no time axis.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A lookup table over future labels.

easy.hint: Same cell repeated T times: same weights or different weights?
easy.explanation: Unrolling exposes the RNN as a weight-tied deep net through time.
easy.deepDive: Unrolling draws the recurrence as T copies of one cell wired in series. All copies share the same matrices, so gradients from every step accumulate into them. This sharing is what lets fixed parameters handle variable lengths.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Steps share weights; separate nets would explode parameters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Unrolling keeps the time axis explicit across T steps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unrolling uses inputs, not future-label lookup.

easy.prompt: What is backpropagation through time (BPTT)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Unroll over T steps, then backprop on that chain (BPTT).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Train each step with a separate unrelated net.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Send gradients only through the last step.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Detach every hidden state to kill gradients.

easy.hint: unfold first, then apply ordinary backprop to which graph?
easy.explanation: BPTT applies the chain rule through the unrolled time graph.
easy.deepDive: BPTT treats the unfolded graph like a T-layer feedforward net. Gradients flow backward through recurrent edges to early steps and shared weights. Memory grows with T, which is why truncation is used on very long sequences.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Shared weights tie all steps into one model.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Earlier steps get gradients via recurrent connections.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Detaching stops BPTT instead of performing it.

easy.prompt: What is the cost of full (non-truncated) BPTT on length-T sequences?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Full history gradients at O(T) memory cost per sequence.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exact gradients with zero memory at any length.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No recurrent connections left in the model.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Guaranteed convex loss in all parameters.

easy.hint: More steps stored means more of what resource consumed?
easy.explanation: Full BPTT is exact but memory-hungry on long sequences.
easy.deepDive: Keeping all T hidden states lets gradients reach arbitrarily early steps exactly. Storing them scales linearly with sequence length and hidden size. Truncated BPTT later trades some of that reach for bounded memory.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Exactness requires storing the full unrolled graph.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Recurrence stays; only the backward horizon could be cut.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: RNN losses remain non-convex regardless of BPTT flavor.

easy.prompt: What does truncated BPTT trade off?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only K-step backward horizon for bounded memory, approximating long credit.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exact infinite-history gradients for free.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deletion of all recurrence from the net.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Freezing the input embeddings forever.

easy.hint: Cut the backward chain short: what is saved and what is lost?
easy.explanation: Truncated BPTT bounds memory by shortening gradient reach.
easy.deepDive: TBPTT cuts the graph every K steps and stops gradients crossing the cut. Updates stay cheap even on streaming text. The price is blindness to dependencies longer than K steps unless states carry them forward.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Truncation approximates; only full BPTT is exact.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Forward recurrence continues; only backward flow is cut.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Embeddings keep training; horizon length is the changed knob.

easy.prompt: What makes data 'sequential' and suitable for an RNN?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Ordered tokens (words, frames, samples) where position carries meaning.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Unordered rows where shuffling changes nothing.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Single fixed vector with no time axis.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Random noise with no learnable structure.

easy.hint: Words in a sentence: does order matter or not?
easy.explanation: Sequence data is ordered; RNNs model position-dependent structure.
easy.deepDive: Language, speech, and sensor streams derive meaning from token order. Shuffling words scrambles sentences, which is why sequence models process positions in order. RNNs consume one element at a time while updating their running state.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Order-free rows suit tabular models, not RNNs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One static vector needs no recurrence over time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Noise has no temporal structure to model.

easy.prompt: In an unrolled RNN, how do shared recurrent weights receive gradients?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Shared weights get gradient contributions summed from every time step.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Each step owns private weights updated only locally.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only the final step contributes any gradient.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Gradients skip shared weights entirely.

easy.hint: One matrix used T times: how many gradient sources does it have?
easy.explanation: Weight tying means gradients accumulate across all steps.
easy.deepDive: Because one matrix serves all steps, its total gradient aggregates how every position used it. Backprop sums these per-step contributions through the unrolled graph. This sharing is what lets fixed parameters learn position-general patterns.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Private weights would defeat the purpose of recurrent sharing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Early steps contribute via the recurrent chain, not just the last one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Shared weights are exactly what BPTT updates.

easy.prompt: What does RNN hidden-state size control?

choices.label: A
choices.body: State dimension caps representable history; bigger states remember more.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Hidden size only changes image brightness.

choices.label: C
choices.body: State size has zero effect on memory capacity.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Bigger states always guarantee perfect recall.

easy.hint: Bigger notebook versus smaller notebook: which holds more notes?
easy.explanation: Hidden size sets the memory bandwidth of the recurrence.
easy.deepDive: The hidden vector is the only channel carrying past into future. Wider states encode richer summaries with less compression loss. Capacity still bounds recall: no finite vector stores unbounded history losslessly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Brightness is image rendering, not recurrent capacity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: State width directly limits representable history.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Larger helps but never guarantees lossless infinite recall.

easy.prompt: How is dropout applied during training versus inference?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Randomly zero activations during training; use the full net at test.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Randomly zero neurons on every test example.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Double the learning rate per layer.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Remove all nonlinear activations.

easy.hint: Train noisy ensemble versus deploy stable predictor: when are masks on?
easy.explanation: Dropout is training-only stochastic masking with test-time disable.
easy.deepDive: Each training step samples a thinned subnetwork, forcing features to be robust without co-adapting. Inverted dropout rescales by 1/(1−p) so expected sums match at inference. At test time masks turn off and the full averaged network predicts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Test-time masking would inject noise into deployed predictions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Learning rate is not touched by dropout masks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Activations stay; only the dropout masks stop.

easy.prompt: Is it true dropout masks should stay on at test time?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No: test-time dropout injects noise and destabilizes predictions.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Yes: always resample masks for every test query.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Yes: bigger dropout at test means better accuracy.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No: dropout should also be deleted during training.

easy.hint: Ensemble average at deploy versus one noisy member: which is stable?
easy.explanation: Standard inference disables dropout; MC dropout is the explicit exception.
easy.deepDive: Dropout trains an implicit ensemble whose average is approximated by the full network. Resampling masks per test query breaks that averaging and adds variance. Monte Carlo dropout is the deliberate exception, sampling many masks to estimate uncertainty.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This is the misconception: masks turn off for standard prediction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: More test noise degrades accuracy instead of helping.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Removing train dropout loses its regularization benefit.

easy.prompt: Why does inverted dropout divide kept activations by (1−p)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Expected sums stay matched so train and test scales agree.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Gradients flow faster through zeroed units.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Test labels leak into the scaling factor.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Weight count doubles automatically.

easy.hint: Drop half the units: what multiplier keeps the expected sum unchanged?
easy.explanation: Inverted dropout rescales survivors to preserve activation expectation.
easy.deepDive: Keeping each unit with probability (1−p) shrinks expected activation sums during training. Dividing survivors by (1−p) restores the original expectation. Inference then needs no rescaling because training already matched the full-network scale.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Zeroed units pass no gradient; scaling fixes expectations, not flow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Scaling uses only the rate p, never any labels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Parameter count is untouched by dropout rescaling.

easy.prompt: What does weight decay do in modern optimizers?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Proportional shrinkage of weights each step (decoupled in AdamW).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Growth of weight magnitudes to fight underfit.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Replacement of gradients with zero vectors.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Random deletion of whole layers per epoch.

easy.hint: Toward zero or away from zero: which direction simplifies?
easy.explanation: Weight decay penalizes large weights to favor simpler models.
easy.deepDive: Decay adds a −ηλw pull toward zero alongside the gradient step. Small weights mean smoother functions that extrapolate less wildly. AdamW separates this pull from adaptive normalization so strength stays predictable.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Decay shrinks weights; growing them is the opposite.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Gradients still drive learning with an extra shrinkage term.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Layer deletion is structural pruning, not decay.

easy.prompt: How is weight decay typically formulated as a penalty?

choices.label: A
choices.body: L2 penalty on weights added to the loss (coupled in SGD, decoupled in AdamW).

choices.label: B
choices.body: L2 distance between train and test images.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Squaring the learning rate each epoch.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Counting the number of nonzero labels.

easy.hint: Penalty on what: weights, images, or learning rates?
easy.explanation: Weight decay is usually an L2-style penalty on parameters.
easy.deepDive: Adding (λ/2)||w||² makes large weights cost loss even when they fit data. SGD applies this gradient directly while AdamW moves it outside normalization. Either way the effect prefers diffuse small weights over spiky large ones.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Image distances are data metrics, not parameter penalties.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Squaring η is a schedule bug, not regularization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Label counts never enter the decay penalty.

easy.prompt: How do you set weight-decay / dropout strength in practice?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Raise λ or dropout when val gap grows; lower them when both losses stall high.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always maximize λ to guarantee generalization.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Set dropout p=1.0 so every unit is dropped.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Tune λ using test-set scores directly.

easy.hint: Gap large versus both bad: which needs more versus less penalty?
easy.explanation: Tune regularization strength against the generalization gap.
easy.deepDive: A widening train-val gap signals overfitting that stronger penalties can close. High losses on both splits signal underfitting where penalties only hurt. Validation curves pick the middle ground instead of blindly maximizing regularization.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Excessive penalty underfits by crushing useful weights.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dropping everything leaves no signal to learn from.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Test scores must never guide hyperparameter choices.

easy.prompt: What are the stages of a sound image data pipeline?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Shuffle, batch, augment-train-only, normalize with train stats, prefetch to GPU.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sort all images by brightness before batching.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Augment test images and report those scores.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Normalize test with test labels mixed in.

easy.hint: Separate train-only transforms from shared batching: which steps leak if shared?
easy.explanation: Clean pipelines randomize, batch, isolate test, and overlap I/O.
easy.deepDive: Shuffling breaks correlation order while batching feeds parallel hardware efficiently. Augmentation and statistic fitting belong to training only to avoid leakage. Prefetching and pinned memory hide I/O latency behind GPU compute.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Brightness sorting biases batches instead of randomizing them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test scores must use clean unseen inputs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Labels must never enter normalization statistics.

easy.prompt: How do you avoid data leakage in preprocessing?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Fitting preprocessing on train only, then applying frozen values to val/test.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Fitting scalers on the full dataset including test.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Recomputing augmentation seeds from test labels.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Shuffling test order to boost accuracy.

easy.hint: Learn statistics from which split if test must stay unseen?
easy.explanation: Prevent leakage by isolating all fitting to training data.
easy.deepDive: Mean, variance, and vocabularies are model knowledge that must come from training data alone. Touching test data during fitting leaks its distribution into the model. Frozen train values keep evaluation honest and deployment-consistent.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That leaks test distribution into the fitted transform.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test labels must never seed training transforms.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Test order cannot change model accuracy.

easy.prompt: Why can random splits overestimate accuracy on grouped data?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Split by group/time (patient, day) so no shared source spans splits.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Shuffle rows randomly ignoring groups.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Duplicate rows across train and test.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Select splits by highest test accuracy.

easy.hint: Same patient in train and test: memorizing whom versus learning what?
easy.explanation: Grouped data needs group-wise splits to test real generalization.
easy.deepDive: Random row splits scatter same-patient or same-day rows across train and test. The model then recognizes sources instead of generalizing to new ones. Group-aware splits force evaluation on truly unseen origins.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ignoring groups is exactly the leakage being fixed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Duplication leaks answers directly across splits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Picking splits by test score is selection bias.

easy.prompt: What is an autoencoder's architecture and objective?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Encoder to bottleneck code, then decoder rebuilding the input.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Generator versus discriminator in a minimax game.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Noise denoising chain reversed step by step.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sorting pixels by brightness into bins.

easy.hint: Compress then rebuild: which two halves does that name?
easy.explanation: Autoencoders learn compressed reconstructions through a bottleneck.
easy.deepDive: The encoder compresses x into a low-dimensional z that keeps only salient structure. The decoder expands z back to reconstruct x as faithfully as possible. Reconstruction error then trains both halves without any labels.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That adversarial game describes GANs, not autoencoders.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Iterative denoising describes diffusion models.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Brightness sorting is not a learned reconstruction.

easy.prompt: Why must a basic autoencoder's bottleneck be constrained?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Bottleneck smaller than input, forcing salient compression.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Hidden code larger than input with no other constraint.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No encoder at all, only a classifier head.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Test labels fed directly into the code.

easy.hint: Copy machine versus compressor: which width forces real compression?
easy.explanation: Undercomplete bottlenecks prevent trivial identity copying.
easy.deepDive: A narrow code cannot memorize every pixel, so training keeps features that reconstruct best. Without constraint a wide hidden layer could learn the identity map trivially. Denoising, sparsity, or variational penalties are alternatives that also block copying.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Unconstrained wide codes can just pass inputs through unchanged.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Classifiers predict labels; autoencoders reconstruct inputs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Codes come from inputs only, never from labels.

easy.prompt: What does a denoising autoencoder train the network to do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Reconstruct corrupted inputs: robust features plus denoising ability.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Memorize noise patterns exactly with no cleanup.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Classify images into labeled categories.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Generate test labels from random seeds.

easy.hint: Input dirty, target clean: what must the net learn to do?
easy.explanation: Denoising autoencoders undo input corruption to learn robust codes.
easy.deepDive: Corrupting x with noise or masking forces the net to use context rather than copying. The learned code captures stable structure that survives perturbation. At inference the same net can clean dirty inputs it never saw clean.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The goal is removing corruption, not memorizing it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reconstruction is unsupervised; no class labels are used.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Outputs are cleaned inputs, not predicted labels.

easy.prompt: How does a variational autoencoder (VAE) differ from a plain autoencoder?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Encoder to (μ,σ), sample z, decode; loss = recon + KL to prior.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Generator fools a discriminator with no encoder.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Pixel sorting with no sampling step.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Hard K-means assignment of each image.

easy.hint: Distribution out, sample in the middle, decode: whose recipe?
easy.explanation: VAEs learn probabilistic codes regularized toward a prior.
easy.deepDive: Encoding distributions instead of points makes the latent space smooth and samplable. The KL term pulls posteriors toward a standard Gaussian prior. New images come from decoding fresh prior samples, not stored examples.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That encoder-free game is the GAN setup.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: VAEs sample continuous codes; they never sort pixels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: K-means makes hard clusters, not smooth generative codes.

easy.prompt: Is it true VAE latent space can be arbitrary and still generate well?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No: arbitrary codes break smoothness; KL shapes a samplable prior geometry.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Yes: any random vector decodes to valid data.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Yes: latent axes always match pixel axes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No: VAE latents must equal test labels.

easy.hint: Random point in an unshaped space: near data or in a hole?
easy.explanation: VAE latents need prior-shaped structure to sample meaningfully.
easy.deepDive: Unregularized codes scatter with holes that decode to garbage when sampled. The KL penalty packs encodings into a dense Gaussian-like ball. Sampling that ball then lands near seen codes and decodes coherently.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This is the misconception: holes in latent space generate nonsense.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Latent axes learn abstract factors, not pixel coordinates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Latents encode content; they never equal labels.

easy.prompt: What is the reparameterization trick in VAEs?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Reparameterize z = μ + σ⊙ε with ε∼N(0,I) so gradients flow.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Stop all gradients at the sampling step.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Replace sampling with argmax lookup.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Copy test images directly into z.

easy.hint: Randomness outside, differentiable path inside: where should noise enter?
easy.explanation: The reparameterization trick makes VAE sampling differentiable.
easy.deepDive: Sampling blocks gradients because it is a stochastic node with no derivative. Moving randomness into an external ε leaves z a differentiable function of μ and σ. Backprop then tunes the encoder through the sampled code.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Blocking gradients would freeze the entire encoder.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Argmax is discrete lookup, not Gaussian sampling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Codes must come from the encoder, never from test data.

easy.prompt: What are a GAN's generator and discriminator?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Generator maps noise z to fakes; discriminator judges real vs fake adversarially.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Encoder compresses inputs to a bottleneck code.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Noise is denoised stepwise into images.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Pixels are clustered with K-means only.

easy.hint: Faker versus detective: which pair matches G and D?
easy.explanation: GANs pit a sampler against a detector in a two-player game.
easy.deepDive: G improves as D's feedback reveals which fakes look implausible. D improves as harder fakes force sharper real-vs-fake boundaries. The minimax game ends ideally with fakes indistinguishable from data samples.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Bottleneck compression is autoencoder territory.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stepwise denoising is the diffusion recipe.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Clustering alone never plays an adversarial game.

easy.prompt: Does the GAN generator see real training data directly?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No: G sees only noise plus D's signal; real data reaches G indirectly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Yes: G is fed real images as its direct input.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Yes: G copies training pixels verbatim.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No: G never learns anything about real data.

easy.hint: Noise in, fakes out: where do real pixels enter the loop?
easy.explanation: Generator learns from discriminator feedback, not direct real-data input.
easy.deepDive: G's input is random noise, never a real example. Real images train D, whose gradients then steer G toward realistic outputs. This indirection is why GANs can invent novel samples instead of retrieving memorized ones.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This is the misconception: only D touches real examples directly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Copying pixels would be memorization, not adversarial learning.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: D's signal carries real-data information back to G.

easy.prompt: How do you generate new images from a trained GAN?

choices.label: A
choices.body: New samples from random z through the trained generator.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Nearest training image retrieved by lookup.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Test labels decoded into pixels.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Random weight matrices printed as images.

easy.hint: Store images or map noise: which creates unseen samples?
easy.explanation: GAN sampling decodes fresh noise vectors into novel outputs.
easy.deepDive: Training shapes G into a map from prior noise to the data manifold. Fresh draws of z land on new points of that manifold. Good GANs interpolate smoothly: nearby z values decode to similar-looking outputs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Retrieval copies old data; generation invents new points.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Labels are not the generator's input.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Weights parameterize the map; noise provides the variation.

medium.prompt: What does the sigmoid activation σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(−z)) do, and where is it most natural?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Sigmoid maps any input to (0,1), useful as a probability-like gate.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sigmoid outputs exactly 0 or 1 for every input.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Sigmoid doubles its input with no bounds.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sigmoid sorts a vector into ranked order.

medium.hint: Plug in very large +z and very large −z: where do the outputs land?
medium.explanation: Sigmoid squashes real values smoothly into the open interval (0,1).
medium.deepDive: The S-shape σ(z)=1/(1+e^(−z)) saturates toward 0 for large negative z and toward 1 for large positive z. That bounded output suits binary probabilities and gates. Saturation also causes tiny gradients at extremes, which is why hidden layers now favor ReLU.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Outputs are continuous between 0 and 1, not hard binary steps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sigmoid is bounded; doubling is a linear map, not a squash.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Ranking a vector is argsort, not an elementwise squash.

medium.prompt: How does tanh differ from sigmoid in output range and centering?

choices.label: A
choices.body: tanh maps inputs to (−1,1) with zero-centered outputs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: tanh maps inputs to (0,1) exactly like a probability.

choices.label: C
choices.body: tanh returns its input unchanged for all z.

choices.label: D
choices.body: tanh outputs integers −1, 0, or 1 only.

medium.hint: Compare ranges: sigmoid is (0,1), so what symmetric range does tanh give?
medium.explanation: tanh is a zero-centered S-curve bounded between −1 and 1.
medium.deepDive: tanh is a rescaled sigmoid: tanh(z)=2σ(2z)−1, so it is steeper and centered at zero. Zero-centered activations help gradient steps because layer outputs average near zero. It still saturates at both ends, so deep stacks can suffer vanishing gradients.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That range describes sigmoid; tanh extends below zero to −1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Identity is the linear map; tanh bends and saturates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: tanh is smooth and continuous, not a three-valued step.

medium.prompt: Why did ReLU largely replace sigmoid/tanh in deep hidden layers?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ReLU returns max(0,z): cheap, nonsaturating for positives, sparsity-inducing.

choices.label: B
choices.body: ReLU returns min(0,z): keeping only negative values.

choices.label: C
choices.body: ReLU squares its input to amplify all magnitudes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: ReLU normalizes each batch to zero mean and unit variance.

medium.hint: Split into cases z>0 and z≤0, then check the slope in each case.
medium.explanation: ReLU passes positives through and zeroes negatives with derivative 0 or 1.
medium.deepDive: For z>0 the derivative is exactly 1, so positive signals flow undiminished through depth. For z≤0 the unit outputs 0, creating sparse activations. The only cost is dead units when a neuron never activates, which variants like Leaky ReLU address.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That flips the function; ReLU keeps positives and kills negatives.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Squaring is a different nonlinearity with exploding magnitudes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Batch statistics describe batchnorm, not an elementwise activation.

medium.prompt: At the output of a classifier, what does softmax over logits z produce?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Softmax turns logits into a probability distribution over classes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Softmax picks the single max logit and discards the rest.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Softmax applies ReLU independently to each logit.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Softmax sorts logits without exponentiating them.

medium.hint: Look for exp plus divide-by-sum: which choice has both steps?
medium.explanation: Softmax exponentiates and normalizes logits into nonnegative values summing to 1.
medium.deepDive: Exponentiating makes every output positive and amplifies gaps between logits. Dividing by the sum forces the vector to add to 1. The result pairs with cross-entropy so gradients push mass toward the true class.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Argmax is hard selection; softmax is a smooth distribution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ReLU acts elementwise with no normalization across classes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sorting reorders; softmax rescales into probabilities.

medium.prompt: Backpropagation computes weight gradients by what mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Analytic gradients via one backward pass using the chain rule.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Numeric slopes by perturbing each weight one at a time.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Random search over weight matrices with no derivatives.

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Count forward passes: one backward sweep versus one perturbation per weight?
medium.explanation: Backprop computes exact gradients for all weights in one reverse sweep.
medium.deepDive: Backprop applies reverse-mode autodiff: each layer multiplies the incoming gradient by its local Jacobian. One backward sweep yields ∂L/∂w for every parameter at roughly the cost of one forward pass. Finite differences would need one extra forward pass per parameter, which is infeasible for millions of weights.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is finite differences, used only for gradient checking on tiny nets.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Random search ignores gradient information entirely.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Clustering is unsupervised grouping, not gradient computation.

medium.prompt: For y=σ(z) with z=wx+b and loss L(y), how does the chain rule give ∂L/∂w?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: ∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂w + ∂L/∂w added to itself twice.

choices.label: C
choices.body: ∂L/∂w = loss value copied directly into each weight.

choices.label: D
choices.body: ∂L/∂w = learning rate times batch size with no graph.

medium.hint: Write loss→activation→affine→weight as nested functions, then differentiate the nest.
medium.explanation: Chain rule multiplies local Jacobians from loss backward to the parameter.
medium.deepDive: Each edge of the computation graph contributes its local derivative, and the chain rule multiplies them from loss back to the weight. Intermediate gradients are reused across parameters sharing upstream paths. This reuse is exactly what makes reverse mode efficient.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Doubling a gradient is not the chain rule; factors come from distinct stages.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Loss is a scalar score; gradients need derivatives, not copies.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Learning rate scales the update step, not the derivative itself.

medium.prompt: What is the standard two-phase order of operations in training an MLP?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Ask what the backward step needs from the forward step to evaluate local derivatives.
medium.explanation: Backprop caches forward values, then propagates gradients backward layer by layer.
medium.deepDive: Forward values like z and σ(z) are cached because local derivatives such as σ′(z) need them. The backward sweep propagates ∂L/∂(layer output) and multiplies by each local Jacobian. Caching trades memory for avoiding a second forward recomputation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Data sampling is independent of the forward/backward algebra.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Updates require gradients, which exist only after the loss is computed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Freezing is a transfer-learning choice, not the backprop order.

medium.prompt: Why is backprop preferred over finite-difference gradient estimates for neural nets?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Compare cost as parameter count grows: linear in P versus roughly constant passes?
medium.explanation: Backprop scales to huge nets; per-weight perturbations do not.
medium.deepDive: Perturbing each weight separately costs one extra forward evaluation per parameter, which is hopeless at deep-learning scale. Backprop reuses shared subpaths to get all gradients in one reverse sweep. Finite differences survive only as a debugging check on tiny models.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Finite differences carry truncation and roundoff error; they only approximate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Per-weight forward passes grow with model size and quickly become infeasible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Backprop handles ReLU via subgradients routinely in every framework.

medium.prompt: What causes vanishing gradients in deep MLPs with saturating activations?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Repeated multiplication by small derivatives shrinks early-layer gradients.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Learning rates that grow exponentially every iteration.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Batch sizes that exceed the dataset size.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Test labels leaking into the training features.

medium.hint: Multiply ten numbers each smaller than 1: what happens to the product?
medium.explanation: Vanishing gradients mean early layers get near-zero signal in deep nets.
medium.deepDive: With saturating activations like sigmoid, each layer's local derivative is at most 0.25, so products over many layers decay exponentially. Early layers then barely move while late layers learn. ReLU, careful init, and normalization were introduced largely to fight this decay.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Growing learning rates cause divergence, not systematic gradient shrinkage.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Oversized batches affect gradient noise, not the chain-rule product decay.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Label leakage is a data bug, not a depth-and-derivative phenomenon.

medium.prompt: Which set of practices actually mitigates vanishing gradients?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Use ReLU, careful initialization, normalization, or residual paths.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Remove all activations and train a deeper linear stack.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Set every weight to the same large constant value.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Zero out all gradients before each optimizer step.

medium.hint: Look for the option that keeps per-layer derivatives near 1 instead of near 0.
medium.explanation: Standard fixes keep gradient magnitudes stable across depth.
medium.deepDive: ReLU keeps derivative 1 for active units so products stop shrinking. He initialization sets the starting variance so signals preserve scale. Normalization and skip connections give gradients shorter or better-conditioned paths backward.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Linear stacks collapse in expressivity and do not fix saturation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Constant init breaks symmetry badly and can explode or stall learning.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Zeroing gradients would stop all learning immediately.

medium.prompt: Loss suddenly NaNs with huge gradient norms in a deep net. Which failure is this?

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Contrast shrinking products with growing ones: which failure spikes the loss?
medium.explanation: Products of large Jacobians amplify gradients exponentially with depth.
medium.deepDive: When recurrent or deep products exceed 1, gradients compound upward instead of decaying. Updates then jump wildly and the loss spikes or NaNs. Gradient clipping caps the step norm to restore stability without changing the loss itself.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Vanishing gives tiny norms and stalled early layers, not NaN spikes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Overfitting is a generalization gap, not a gradient-magnitude blowup.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Underfitting shows flat high losses, not sudden divergence.

medium.prompt: Early layers learn far slower than late layers in a deep sigmoid MLP. What is the likely culprit?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Check each activation's derivative: which one is ~0 in its current regime?
medium.explanation: Saturated sigmoids have near-zero local slope, starving upstream layers.
medium.deepDive: Sigmoid derivatives peak at 0.25 and fall toward 0 in the tails, so saturated units pass almost no gradient. Deep stacks multiply many such small factors. ReLU or normalization moves operating points back to regions with usable slope.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Active ReLUs have derivative 1 and preserve gradient flow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Linear outputs have constant slope and do not saturate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Skips add identity paths that help, not hurt, gradient flow.

medium.prompt: How does SGD with momentum change the plain SGD update?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Velocity accumulating past gradients to push through noise and ravines.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Random restarts of weights every iteration.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Sorting gradients by magnitude before applying them.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Zeroing gradients whenever loss decreases.

medium.hint: Average noisy steps over time: does direction get steadier or jumpier?
medium.explanation: Momentum smooths updates by reusing a running average of gradients.
medium.deepDive: Momentum keeps an exponential moving average v ← μv + g and steps along v instead of raw g. Consistent directions build speed while opposing noise cancels. The coefficient μ near 0.9 sets how much history persists.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Restarts discard progress; momentum preserves directional history.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sorting coordinates has no role in momentum accumulation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Zeroing on progress would halt learning exactly when it works.

medium.prompt: Why does momentum help in narrow-valley (ill-conditioned) loss landscapes?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Dampens zigzag across steep walls while accelerating along the valley floor.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Increases oscillation on every axis equally.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Freezes movement along all flat directions.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Removes the need for any learning rate.

medium.hint: Average +g then −g across the ravine: what survives?
medium.explanation: Momentum averages out opposing components and reinforces consistent ones.
medium.deepDive: In ravines, cross-valley gradients alternate sign and cancel in the running average. Down-valley gradients persist and accumulate into speed. The result is faster progress with less bouncing than vanilla SGD.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Averaging reduces zigzag; it does not amplify it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Flat consistent directions accumulate speed rather than freezing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Velocity still scales by the learning rate.

medium.prompt: How does Nesterov accelerated gradient differ from classical momentum?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Evaluate gradient at a lookahead point: w + μv, then correct velocity.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Evaluate gradient twice at the same point and average.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Skip the backward pass every other iteration.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Apply momentum only to biases, never to weights.

medium.hint: Where should you measure the slope: behind the ball or ahead of it?
medium.explanation: Nesterov momentum looks ahead, giving a corrective gradient.
medium.deepDive: Nesterov peeks ahead along current velocity before computing the gradient. This anticipatory correction slows the ball before overshooting minima. It often converges slightly faster and more stably than classical momentum.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Duplicating the same gradient adds no lookahead information.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Skipping backward passes drops needed gradient signal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Momentum applies to all parameters, not biases alone.

medium.prompt: What does the momentum coefficient μ control in practice?

choices.label: A
choices.body: μ near 0.9 keeps useful history; μ near 1.0 can overshoot and oscillate.

choices.label: B
choices.body: μ must always equal exactly 0 for any learning.

choices.label: C
choices.body: μ counts the number of training examples.

choices.label: D
choices.body: μ sets the batch size automatically.

medium.hint: More history means more speed but also more inertia: what breaks?
medium.explanation: Momentum coefficient trades smoothing against overshoot risk.
medium.deepDive: Higher μ lengthens memory, smoothing noise but risking slingshots past minima. Zero μ reduces to plain SGD with no averaging benefit. Tuning μ alongside η balances speed against overshoot for each landscape.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Zero momentum is just SGD; nonzero values are the standard setting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dataset size is independent of the velocity decay factor.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Batch size is chosen separately from the momentum coefficient.

medium.prompt: How does Adam differ from SGD with momentum?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Per-parameter adaptive steps from first- and second-moment estimates.

choices.label: B
choices.body: One global step size identical for every parameter forever.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Gradient-free random perturbations with no moments.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exact Hessian inverses computed each iteration.

medium.hint: Which optimizer keeps two moving averages per weight: mean and uncentered variance?
medium.explanation: Adam adapts each parameter's step using running gradient moments.
medium.deepDive: Adam tracks m for direction and v for per-coordinate scale, updating w by m̂/(√v̂+ε). Busy parameters get smaller effective steps and quiet ones larger. Bias correction fixes the zero-initialized early estimates.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A single global step is SGD's style, not Adam's adaptivity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Adam is gradient-based; it never uses gradient-free search.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Adam is first-order; it never inverts Hessians.

medium.prompt: What is Adam's bias correction and why does it exist?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Reset moments to random values each step.

choices.label: D

medium.hint: If an average starts at 0, are early values too small or too big?
medium.explanation: Bias correction rescales early moment estimates toward their true values.
medium.deepDive: Moments start at zero, so early averages underestimate the true moments by a factor of (1−βᵗ). Dividing removes that cold-start drag. Without correction, the first steps would be far too small.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Scaling by epoch number would explode moments over time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Random resets would destroy the running statistics.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Dataset size never enters the bias-correction formula.

medium.prompt: Is it true that Adam needs no learning-rate tuning?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Adam provably needs zero tuning on every task ever.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Adam tunes itself by reading test labels.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Adam sets batch size and depth automatically.

medium.hint: Adaptive per-coordinate scale still multiplies which global knob?
medium.explanation: Adam reduces sensitivity but the learning rate still needs tuning.
medium.deepDive: Adaptivity rescales coordinates but the global η still sets overall stride. Tasks differ in curvature, noise, and batch size, so defaults transfer only roughly. Papers routinely grid-search η even when keeping β₁, β₂ fixed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This is the exact misconception: η still matters greatly in practice.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Adam never touches test labels; tuning uses validation loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Architecture and batching stay human-chosen hyperparameters.

medium.prompt: What role does Adam's ε hyperparameter play?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: ε shuffles the dataset before each epoch.

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Look at m̂/(√v̂+ε): what happens when the denominator nears zero?
medium.explanation: Adam's ε stabilizes division and modulates how adaptive steps are.
medium.deepDive: The update divides by √v̂+ε, so ε floors the denominator for near-zero second moments. Tiny defaults like 1e-8 preserve strong adaptivity. Raising ε toward 1e-3 or higher dampens the normalization and behaves more like momentum SGD.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Epoch count is scheduled separately from ε.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Shuffling is data pipeline logic, not denominator damping.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Freezing is pruning or dropout behavior, not ε.

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Which curve starts high, falls smoothly, and flattens at the bottom?
medium.explanation: Cosine annealing decays LR smoothly along a cosine curve.
medium.deepDive: Cosine annealing follows half a cosine wave from peak η down to η_min. Early large values explore while late small values refine. Restarts (warm restarts) can repeat the wave to hop between basins.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Constant η is the no-schedule baseline, not annealing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Raising η on plateaus is a different heuristic, not cosine decay.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Schedules change step size, never zero the weights.

medium.explanation: Step schedules cut LR at fixed epoch milestones.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The loss stays fixed; only the step size changes.

medium.explanation: Gradient clipping bounds step size to prevent explosion instability.
medium.deepDive: Exploding gradients produce enormous steps that fling weights into bad regions. Rescaling oversized gradients to norm τ preserves their direction while bounding stride. Clipping is standard insurance for RNNs and very deep nets.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Clipping works with any optimizer and is not a Newton switch.

medium.explanation: Batch size trades hardware efficiency against update count and sharpness.
medium.deepDive: Large batches cut gradient noise and parallelize well, but they take fewer steps per epoch. Without raising η or adding epochs, they can settle into sharper minima. Linear LR scaling plus warmup is the standard compensation.

medium.deepDive: A 1×1 kernel looks at one spatial location across all input channels and projects to new channels. It adds depth and nonlinearity cheaply without widening spatial context. Bottleneck blocks sandwich 3×3 convs between 1×1 shrink and expand steps.

medium.explanation: VGG builds depth from uniform small-kernel stacks.

choices.label: D
