medium.hint: Biggest stretch factor of a matrix: which norm is that?
medium.explanation: Spectral norm caps discriminator sensitivity for stable GAN gradients.
medium.deepDive: Dividing each matrix by its spectral norm caps how fast D's output can change with inputs. Lipschitz-bounded critics give smoother, more stable gradients to G. The power-iteration estimate makes the constraint cheap per step.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Zero LR would halt all discriminator learning.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Positivity is an activation choice, not a norm constraint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Batch and vocabulary sizes are unrelated to spectral norms.

medium.prompt: Why do vanilla VAE samples often look blurry next to GAN samples?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Blurry averages from pixel-wise loss hedging over plausible details.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Perfectly sharp samples in every run.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Exact memorization of training pixels.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No outputs at all from the decoder.

medium.hint: Average ten sharp faces: sharp or blurry mean face?
medium.explanation: VAE reconstructions blur because MSE averages over uncertainty.
medium.deepDive: Mean squared error rewards the average of possible sharp reconstructions. Averaging edges and textures produces characteristic VAE softness. GAN and diffusion objectives score realism instead, yielding crisper samples at higher training cost.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Sharpness is the known VAE weakness, not its signature.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Blurriness comes from averaging, not from copying pixels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Decoders do output images, just smoothed ones.

medium.prompt: What does the β coefficient control in a β-VAE?

choices.label: A
choices.body: β balances reconstruction fidelity against prior-matching/KL pressure.

choices.label: B
choices.body: β sets the batch size automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: β shuffles latent axes randomly.

choices.label: D
choices.body: β deletes the decoder network.

medium.hint: Weight on KL up: codes more prior-like or more data-like?
medium.explanation: β-VAE weight trades latent structure against reconstruction quality.
medium.deepDive: Higher β squeezes codes toward the prior, often disentangling factors but degrading detail. Lower β frees reconstruction at the cost of hole-ridden latents. β-VAE search picks the trade-off that keeps samples coherent yet informative.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Batch size is set independently of β.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Axis order is arbitrary; β does not permute it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The decoder stays essential for reconstruction.

medium.prompt: VAE trains with KL term ≈ 0 and z manipulations change nothing. Diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Posterior collapse: decoder ignores z; fix with KL annealing, free bits, stronger decoders.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Perfect latent usage needing no fix.

choices.label: C
choices.body: GPU overheating from large batches.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Test labels appearing in the latent code.

medium.hint: KL near zero with good recon: is z used or ignored?
medium.explanation: KL-vanishing means the VAE decoder bypasses its latent code.
medium.deepDive: Overpowered autoregressive decoders can model data without consulting z, driving KL to zero. Annealing β from 0 lets codes become useful before regularization bites. Architectural limits on the decoder also force reliance on the latent path.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ignored latents are a failure, not a success.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Hardware heat cannot zero out the KL term selectively.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Labels never enter the unsupervised latent path.

medium.prompt: What are diffusion models' forward and reverse processes?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Gradually add Gaussian noise (forward), then learn step-wise denoising (reverse).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sort pixels once with no learned steps.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Cluster images with K-means and stop.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Copy training images into the output folder.

medium.hint: Destroy slowly, then learn to rebuild step by step: whose loop?
medium.explanation: Diffusion pairs a fixed noising process with learned denoising.
medium.deepDive: The fixed forward chain destroys structure on a known schedule until only noise remains. A network then learns each small denoising jump conditioned on timestep. Sampling starts from pure noise and applies those jumps back to data.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Single sorting has no learned generative chain.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Clustering groups data; it does not synthesize new samples.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Copying is retrieval, not iterative generation.

medium.prompt: What target does a denoising diffusion network learn to predict?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Predict the added noise (or clean mean) at each timestep, averaged over noise levels.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Classify images into labeled classes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Predict test-set indices directly.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Maximize discriminator fooling rate only.

medium.hint: Known noise added means known noise can be the target: predict what?
medium.explanation: Diffusion training supervises denoising with self-generated noise targets.
medium.deepDive: Noising x_0 with known ε creates supervised pairs of (noisy x_t, target ε) for free. The network learns one denoiser shared across timesteps via time embeddings. At sampling, subtracting predicted noise iteratively reveals clean structure.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Diffusion training is unsupervised denoising, not classification.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test indices never appear in diffusion objectives.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No discriminator participates in diffusion training.

medium.prompt: Why is diffusion sampling slow yet high-quality?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Many small steps: quality and diversity at high sampling cost.

choices.label: B
choices.body: One argmax with zero sampling cost always.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No steps at all, output pure noise.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Copying the nearest training image.

medium.hint: Many careful cleanups versus one giant leap: which stays on-manifold?
medium.explanation: Diffusion sampling trades step count for sample quality.
medium.deepDive: Each reverse step removes a little noise, so errors stay small and controllable. Hundreds of steps compound into sharp coherent samples covering many modes. Distillation and fast samplers cut steps by approximating the same trajectory cheaply.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Single jumps cannot invert the gradual noising chain well.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Pure noise is the starting point, not the output.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Diffusion synthesizes novel points rather than retrieving.

medium.prompt: What does Wasserstein (WGAN) loss change about GAN training?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Real-vs-fake score gap (earth-mover distance) for smoother G gradients.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Pixel-wise L2 between each fake and a random real image.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Classification accuracy of G on labeled classes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Parameter count of D as the training signal.

medium.hint: Saturated sigmoid versus unbounded score: which keeps gradients alive?
medium.explanation: WGAN replaces saturating probabilities with a smooth transport-distance signal.
medium.deepDive: Wasserstein critics output unbounded scores instead of probabilities, so gradients stay informative even when fakes are far from reals. Weight clipping or gradient penalties enforce the Lipschitz condition the distance needs. Training stabilizes at the cost of extra critic steps per generator step.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Random pixel pairing is not a distribution distance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: G has no class labels in the unconditional WGAN setup.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Parameter counts never serve as loss signals.

medium.prompt: How do you sample brand-new images from a trained VAE?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Draw z ∼ N(0,I) and decode it with the trained decoder.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Retrieve the nearest training image by pixel distance.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Feed test labels into the encoder as input.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Print encoder weight matrices as grayscale images.

medium.hint: Trained toward what distribution: prior ball or training pixels?
medium.explanation: VAE generation samples the prior and decodes new points.
medium.deepDive: The KL term shaped encodings to fill the prior ball densely during training. Fresh prior draws therefore land near familiar codes. Decoding them yields novel images blending learned factors rather than stored copies.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Retrieval copies old data instead of synthesizing new points.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Labels never enter VAE sampling; the prior draw does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Weights parameterize decoding; noise provides the novelty.

medium.prompt: Why do diffusion networks take the timestep t as input?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Timestep embeddings telling the net the current noise level.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Test labels concatenated to every pixel.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Frozen random outputs ignoring the timestep.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A separate full network per timestep with no sharing.

medium.hint: Same net, different noise levels: what extra input disambiguates them?
medium.explanation: Diffusion nets condition on timestep to share one denoiser across noise levels.
medium.deepDive: Denoising jumps differ hugely between near-clean and near-noise inputs. Sinusoidal or learned time embeddings condition shared layers on t. One network then serves all timesteps instead of needing hundreds of copies.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Test labels never enter diffusion conditioning.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ignoring t would force one jump size for all noise levels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sharing with time conditioning is the efficient standard design.

hard.prompt: What is the goal of Xavier/He weight initialization in MLPs?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Symmetry breaking with controlled variance so signals neither vanish nor explode.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Identical constant weights so every neuron learns the same feature.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Enormous initial weights so activations start saturated.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Zeroing all biases to exactly NaN before training.

hard.hint: Ask what two jobs init must do: break ties and preserve signal scale.
hard.explanation: Good initialization randomizes with variance matched to layer width and activation.
hard.deepDive: Random sampling makes neurons start different so they can diversify during training. Scaling variance by fan-in/fan-out keeps forward activations and backward gradients at stable magnitudes. Xavier suits tanh/sigmoid while He suits ReLU's halved activation rate.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Identical weights keep neurons synchronized forever; no diversity emerges.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Huge weights saturate activations and destabilize early gradients.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: NaN biases corrupt every computation; biases usually start at zero.

hard.prompt: For a deep ReLU MLP, which initialization scaling is correct and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: He (variance 2/fan-in) because ReLU zeroes about half its inputs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All weights set to 1.0 so every layer is deterministic.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Weights sampled with variance 100 regardless of width.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Dataset pixel means copied directly into weights.

hard.hint: Count surviving activations after ReLU: what fraction remains, and what scaling fixes it?
hard.explanation: He scaling compensates for ReLU discarding half the activations on average.
hard.deepDive: ReLU kills negatives, halving activation variance relative to symmetric nonlinearities. Doubling the weight variance compensates so forward magnitudes stay stable. Xavier's 1/fan-in scaling would leave ReLU nets too small and slow to train.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Constant weights preserve symmetry; hidden units never diversify.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Width-blind huge variance explodes activations in wide layers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Data means carry no architectural fan-in information for variance control.

hard.prompt: Which initialization keeps all hidden units in a layer stuck computing the same function?

choices.label: A
choices.body: All-zero initialization: every hidden unit computes the same gradient and never diversifies.

choices.label: B
choices.body: He initialization: units diversify and signals keep scale.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Pretrained transfer weights: features start useful and diverse.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Small random init: symmetry breaks and training proceeds.

hard.hint: Trace two neurons starting equal: do their gradients ever differ?
hard.explanation: Zero init is the classic symmetry failure: identical units stay identical.
hard.deepDive: With identical weights, every neuron in a layer sees the same forward value and the same backward gradient. Gradient descent then updates them identically forever. Random init is required precisely to escape this symmetry trap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: He init randomizes, so units diverge toward different features.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Pretrained weights are already diverse from prior training.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Small random values break symmetry by construction.

hard.prompt: Why is reverse-mode autodiff the efficient choice for neural network training?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Reverse mode: one backward pass gives all parameter gradients for a scalar loss.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Forward mode: one pass per parameter gives all gradients cheapest.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Symbolic integration of the dataset with no graph traversal.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exhaustive grid search over every weight value.

hard.hint: Compare input count (millions) to output count (one loss): which mode scales with outputs?
hard.explanation: Backprop is reverse-mode autodiff, optimal for many-params-to-one-loss maps.
hard.deepDive: Neural losses map millions of parameters to one scalar, which is exactly the regime where reverse mode wins. Forward mode would need a sweep per parameter to build the same Jacobian. Frameworks therefore record the forward graph and replay it backward once.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Forward mode scales with parameter count; it suits few-inputs-many-outputs maps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Autodiff traverses computation graphs; it does not symbolically integrate data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Grid search is exponential in parameters and never used for deep nets.

hard.prompt: When is finite-difference gradient estimation actually appropriate in deep learning?

choices.label: A
choices.body: To verify backprop on a tiny subnet, accepting slower per-weight cost.

choices.label: B
choices.body: To train a billion-parameter model faster than backprop.

choices.label: C
choices.body: To replace the loss function with random guessing.

choices.label: D
choices.body: To eliminate all floating-point error from training.

hard.hint: Think debug-time versus train-time: when is O(P) forward passes acceptable?
hard.explanation: Gradient checking uses finite differences as a slow correctness check.
hard.deepDive: Finite differences approximate each partial derivative by (L(w+ε)−L(w−ε))/2ε, which is simple but needs extra forward passes per parameter. On a handful of weights that cost is affordable for debugging. Agreement with backprop within tolerance confirms the analytic implementation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Per-weight passes are hopeless at billion-parameter scale.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Finite differences still need the real loss; they do not replace it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Finite differences add truncation error; they are less exact, not error-free.

hard.prompt: Forward-mode versus reverse-mode autodiff differ in what?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Jacobian accumulation order: backward (reverse) versus forward through the graph.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Whether the learning rate schedule is cosine or step decay.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Whether dropout masks are resampled each batch.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Whether images are padded with zeros or reflected.

hard.hint: Same chain-rule factors, different multiplication order: what varies?
hard.explanation: Forward vs reverse mode differ in traversal direction, not in math results.
hard.deepDive: Both modes apply the same chain rule factors, so exact arithmetic would agree. They differ only in which direction Jacobian products accumulate across the graph. Reverse mode reuses the loss-side vector once, while forward mode pushes one perturbation per parameter.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Schedules scale update steps; they are unrelated to differentiation mode.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dropout is stochastic regularization, not a differentiation traversal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Padding is input geometry, not Jacobian accumulation order.

hard.prompt: 75% of ReLUs in a deep MLP output 0 on all inputs with no recovery. Diagnosis and fix?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Many ReLUs stuck outputting 0 with zero gradient: lower LR or use Leaky ReLU/better init.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Perfect convergence: raise the learning rate immediately.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Label noise: relabel the entire dataset by hand.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Too much data: delete half the training set.

hard.hint: If output is always 0, what is ReLU's local derivative there?
hard.explanation: Dead ReLUs never activate, so they pass no gradient and stop learning.
hard.deepDive: Large updates can push biases so negative that units never activate again, freezing their gradients at 0. Monitoring the fraction of active ReLUs reveals the die-off. Smaller steps, careful init, or a small negative slope keeps units alive.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Raising LR worsens die-off by pushing units further negative.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Uniform zero activations indicate dead units, not wrong labels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Removing data cannot revive units whose gradients are zero.

hard.prompt: Activation histograms in a tanh MLP pile at −1 and +1 with stalled learning. What does this show?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Saturated tanh/sigmoid outputs near ±1/0/1 with tiny local slopes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Softmax probabilities that sum exactly to 1.0.

choices.label: C
choices.body: ReLU outputs growing linearly with positive inputs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Zero training loss with perfect accuracy.

hard.hint: Match histogram shape to derivative size: where are these activations' slopes?
hard.explanation: Extreme-piled activations signal saturation and near-zero derivatives.
hard.deepDive: Flat activation histograms piled at the extremes mean pre-activations live in the tails. There the derivatives σ′(z) and tanh′(z) approach 0, choking gradient flow. Recentering with normalization or switching to ReLU restores usable slope.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Softmax summing to 1 is required behavior, not saturation evidence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Linear ReLU growth is the healthy nonsaturating regime.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Perfect training fit contradicts the reported stall.

hard.prompt: How do you confirm vanishing gradients versus other training failures in a deep MLP?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Plot gradient norms per layer: decay toward input confirms vanishing; add skips/norm/ReLU.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Delete early layers until norms look equal.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Increase batch size until norms equalize by definition.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Shuffle test labels to rebalance the gradient flow.

hard.hint: What measurement separates 'early layers get nothing' from other failures?
hard.explanation: Layerwise gradient norms diagnose vanishing versus healthy flow.
hard.deepDive: Healthy nets show roughly comparable gradient magnitudes across layers. Exponential decay from output to input is the fingerprint of vanishing gradients. Architectural fixes shorten the effective backward path rather than merely tuning the batch.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Deleting layers dodges depth instead of diagnosing gradient flow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Batch size changes noise, not the layerwise decay signature.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Corrupting labels harms training and reveals nothing about norms.

hard.prompt: How does AdamW decouple weight decay from Adam's adaptive step?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Decay weights directly each step, outside Adam's adaptive rescaling.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Delete momentum estimates and use plain SGD.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Invert the Hessian matrix every iteration.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Set all adaptive rates to zero permanently.

hard.hint: Where should shrinkage apply: inside the normalized gradient or directly on w?
hard.explanation: AdamW separates weight decay from the adaptive gradient normalization.
hard.deepDive: Classic Adam adds L2 to the gradient, which its normalization then distorts unequally across parameters. AdamW instead does w ← w − ηλw separately after the adaptive step. This decoupling restores proper regularization strength and improves generalization.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: AdamW keeps both moment estimates; only the decay placement changes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: AdamW stays first-order; no Hessian inverse appears.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Adaptive scaling remains active in AdamW.

hard.prompt: Why does L2-in-Adam behave differently from decoupled weight decay?

choices.label: A
choices.body: L2-inside-gradient gets normalized unevenly; decoupled decay fixes regularization strength.

choices.label: B
choices.body: L2 always causes immediate divergence in Adam.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Decoupling removes all hyperparameters from training.

choices.label: D
choices.body: AdamW only works on linear models.

hard.hint: Track an L2 term through division by √v̂: does every weight feel equal decay?
hard.explanation: AdamW fixes the distortion of L2 regularization by adaptive denominators.
hard.deepDive: Because Adam divides by √v̂, an L2 term mixed into g is rescaled differently per coordinate. Strongly-updated weights feel less decay than intended. Applying λw directly makes shrinkage uniform and predictable across parameters.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: L2-in-Adam trains but regularizes unevenly; it does not always diverge.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: AdamW still needs η, λ, and moment hyperparameters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: AdamW is standard for transformers and CNNs, not just linear models.

hard.prompt: What kind of minima does sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) seek?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Flat regions robust to small perturbations, not just low loss points.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Points with maximal training loss.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Points with exactly zero gradient norm everywhere.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Points needing no validation data at all.

hard.hint: Low loss in a pit versus on a plateau: which survives small bumps?
hard.explanation: Sharpness-aware minimization favors wide, robust minima.
hard.deepDive: SAM minimizes the worst-case loss inside a small neighborhood around w. Flat minima tolerate data and parameter shifts better than sharp pits. The extra ascent-then-descent step costs compute but often boosts generalization.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: SAM still minimizes loss; it penalizes sharpness around the minimum.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Gradients are generally nonzero during the SAM neighborhood search.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Validation remains the way to confirm generalization gains.

hard.prompt: What does batch normalization compute during training?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Per-channel batch mean/variance, then learned scale γ and shift β.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Full test-set statistics applied during training.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Fixed constants chosen once before training.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Gradients of the loss with respect to labels.

hard.hint: Normalize first, then ask what relearns the scale: γ and what?
hard.explanation: BatchNorm normalizes with batch stats plus an affine restore step.
hard.deepDive: Normalizing each channel to zero mean and unit variance stabilizes layer input distributions. The learnable γ and β let the network restore any needed scale or offset. This smoothing permits higher learning rates and faster convergence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Test stats are unseen; training uses current-batch statistics.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Batch stats change every step; they are not fixed constants.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Norm uses activations, never gradients with respect to labels.

hard.prompt: Why does batchnorm use running statistics at inference instead of batch stats?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Running averages of μ and σ, since single/batch stats are noisy or undefined.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Fresh gradients computed from test labels.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Dropout masks resampled from test targets.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Batch size forced to exactly 32 at inference.

hard.hint: What breaks when the 'batch' is one example at deployment?
hard.explanation: Inference uses running stats for stable, deterministic normalization.
hard.deepDive: With batch size 1 there is no meaningful batch variance to normalize by. Running averages collected during training approximate population statistics. Freezing to these averages keeps inference deterministic and batch-independent.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inference uses no labels or gradients at all.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dropout is disabled at inference; it is unrelated to BN stats.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Convs run at any batch size; BN needs consistent population stats.

hard.prompt: How does layer normalization differ from batch normalization?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Across features per example, so it works with batch size 1 and RNNs/transformers.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Across the batch, requiring thousands of examples.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only on the final softmax outputs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Using test labels to compute variance.

hard.hint: Which dimension survives when batch size is 1: batch or feature?
hard.explanation: LayerNorm normalizes per example over features, not over the batch.
hard.deepDive: LayerNorm computes μ and σ over the feature dimension of each token or example independently. Batch size never enters, so tiny or variable batches are fine. That batch-independence is why transformers and recurrent models prefer it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes batchnorm's weakness; layer norm avoids batch dependence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: LayerNorm sits inside blocks on hidden states, not only at softmax.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Normalization uses activations only, never labels.

hard.prompt: Training loss keeps dropping but validation plateaus early. What is the disciplined next step?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Immediately switch to random search with no gradients.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Delete the validation set to remove the gap.

choices.label: D

hard.hint: Separate under-optimization (both bad) from overfitting (train good, val bad): which is this?
hard.explanation: Diagnose optimization settings before adding regularization or data.
hard.deepDive: A stalled validator while training improves signals overfitting or an η too small to escape. First verify the schedule and momentum settings are sane. Then add weight decay, augmentation, or dropout, since deleting validation only hides the problem.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Gradient methods still work; random search wastes the signal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Removing validation hides overfitting instead of fixing it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Freezing stops all progress rather than diagnosing the gap.

hard.prompt: What is a sound order for tuning optimizer hyperparameters?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

hard.explanation: Tune the highest-leverage knob (η) first, guided by validation.
hard.deepDive: Learning rate dominates outcomes, so it gets the first search budget. Momentum and Adam betas refine the trajectory afterward. Validation curves reveal overfitting and instability that training loss alone conceals.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test scores must never guide tuning; use validation only.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tasks differ in curvature and noise, so blind copying misfires.

hard.prompt: When scaling to very large batches, what adjustment preserves training behavior?

choices.label: A

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

hard.hint: Less noise per step allows what change to stride length?
hard.explanation: Large-batch training needs proportional LR scaling and warmup.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fixed η with huge batches under-steps and shifts the optimum basin.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Model capacity is independent of batch-size scaling rules.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Normalization still helps large-batch optimization; do not remove it.

hard.prompt: What does effective receptive field analysis reveal versus theoretical size?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every RF pixel contributes exactly equally.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.body: Pooling never changes which pixels matter.

hard.hint: Overlapping windows pile up most in the middle: where is influence strongest?

hard.prompt: How are generative models evaluated beyond eyeballing samples?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Sample quality plus diversity and likelihood where tractable.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Training loss alone with no samples inspected.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Parameter count as the only metric.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Test-label memorization rate.

hard.hint: Good-looking but identical samples: quality high, what else low?
hard.explanation: Generative evaluation balances fidelity, diversity, and density fit.
hard.deepDive: FID and Inception Score compare feature statistics of fakes versus reals for vision. Precision-recall splits quality from coverage so collapse is caught. Likelihood-based models additionally report bits-per-dim where exact densities exist.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Loss alone hides mode dropping and perceptual quality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Size never measures output distribution match.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Memorization is a failure, not an evaluation goal.

hard.prompt: What do precision and recall mean for generative evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Precision (fidelity) versus recall (coverage) of the real manifold.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Train accuracy versus test accuracy only.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Weight magnitude versus gradient norm.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Batch size versus learning rate.

hard.hint: Realistic fakes versus all real modes covered: which two axes?
hard.explanation: Precision/recall for GANs separates quality from diversity.
hard.deepDive: Precision asks whether each fake looks like a real example. Recall asks whether real variety appears among the fakes. Reporting both exposes models that are sharp but collapsed versus diverse but blurry.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Classifier accuracy splits do not measure distribution coverage.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Weight statistics are optimization diagnostics, not sample metrics.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Batch and LR settings never score generated distributions.

hard.prompt: How do conditional GANs / guided diffusion control what gets generated?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Condition on labels/text, or guide sampling toward desired attributes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Delete all conditioning signals permanently.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Train only on test labels directly.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Fix the noise seed to one constant.

hard.hint: Same noise, different requested class: what extra input changes the output?
hard.explanation: Conditional generation steers outputs via side information and guidance.
hard.deepDive: Class embeddings, text encoders, or attribute codes steer generation toward requested content. Classifier or classifier-free guidance scales how strongly samples obey the condition. Unconditional models instead sample whatever the prior emphasizes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Removing conditioning destroys controllability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test labels must never become training conditions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One fixed seed yields one output, not controllable variety.

hard.prompt: How do generative latent codes differ from self-supervised features?

choices.label: A
choices.body: VAE/GAN latents compress + sample; SSL features discriminate via frozen probes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: They are identical methods with identical goals.

choices.label: C
choices.body: SSL generates sharper images than any GAN.

choices.label: D
choices.body: VAEs cannot learn any useful features.

hard.hint: Sample new data versus separate classes linearly: same representation goal?
hard.explanation: Generative versus self-supervised codes serve different downstream ends.
hard.deepDive: Generative codes optimize reconstruction or realism, which need not align with class boundaries. Contrastive and masked features optimize discriminability of instances or context directly. Hybrid models therefore pair generative decoding with discriminative losses.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Objectives and evaluations differ fundamentally across the two families.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sharpness belongs to GAN/diffusion claims, not SSL generally.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: VAE codes do transfer, just less directly than contrastive ones.

hard.prompt: What is the core trade-off choosing VAE vs GAN vs diffusion?

choices.label: A
choices.body: VAE stable but blurry; GAN sharp but unstable; diffusion sharp/stable but slow.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All three train identically with identical trade-offs.

choices.label: C
choices.body: VAEs never train; GANs never sample.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Speed and quality never trade off anywhere.

hard.hint: Stable-blurry, sharp-finicky, sharp-slow: match families to slots.
hard.explanation: Model families trade stability, sharpness, and sampling cost.
hard.deepDive: VAE likelihood training converges reliably but pixel averaging softens outputs. GAN adversaries sharpen at the price of mode collapse and tuning pain. Diffusion chains stabilize likelihood-style training with iterative refinement costing many sampling steps.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Training dynamics and sampling costs differ sharply across families.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: All three families train and sample in practice.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sampling cost versus quality is the central tension.

hard.prompt: How do you interpolate between two generated samples meaningfully?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Interpolate codes or noise and decode each step for smooth morphs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Average raw pixels of two images directly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Swap weight matrices between models.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sort images by file size and blend.

hard.hint: Blend in code space then decode, or blend pixels: which morphs semantically?
hard.explanation: Latent interpolation tests generative-space continuity.
hard.deepDive: Well-shaped latent spaces map nearby codes to similar outputs. Walking the segment between two codes visits plausible intermediates. Smooth morphs therefore diagnose continuity while jumps reveal holes in the learned manifold.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Pixel averaging ghosts instead of morphing semantics.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Weight swapping mixes models, not samples.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: File size ordering has no generative meaning.
